title: Why is Islam strong despite differences of opinion among Muslims?
headline: The four schools treat their disagreements as a mercy while condemning sectarian division

summary.text: The four schools of law hold that their differing over derived rulings does not remove those who differ from the fold, and each school's own literature describes that disagreement as a mercy or an expansion for people. The Quran and the hadith are read as distinguishing a difference of understanding, in which each side has an excuse, from partisanship over fundamentals, which is what the Quran condemns. The slogan "the disagreement of my ummah is a mercy" is not authentic as a prophetic saying, yet scholars keep its substance while grounding it in the two-rewards hadith and in the Companions' practice.

paragraphs.text: The Quran commands unity around the revealed core: "And hold firmly to the rope of Allāh all together and do not become divided" (Quran 3:103), followed two verses later by a warning against those "who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them" (Quran 3:105), with the tafsir tying that blame to splitting into sects and parties over fundamentals. It also gives a procedure for legitimate difference: "And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allāh and the Messenger" (Quran 4:59), which treats disagreement as a normal event with a mechanism rather than a sin in itself.

Surat al-Ma'idah says "To each of you We prescribed a law and a method," then explains that had He willed He would have made humanity one nation, "but [He intended] to test you in what He has given you; so race to [all that is] good" (Quran 5:48). The tafsir given for the verse says Allah deliberately made the codes differ in order to test who obeys, and that the differing parties return to Him for the final verdict. Surat Hud repeats the theme: "And if your Lord had willed, He could have made mankind one community; but they will not cease to differ, except whom your Lord has given mercy" (Quran 11:118-119).

Where the Quran uses its harshest language it names the cause: differing "after knowledge had come to them, out of jealous animosity between themselves" (Quran 2:213, 42:14, 45:17), and factions that "divided their religion among them into portions, each faction, in what it has, rejoicing" (Quran 23:53; also 30:32). Scholars draw the line there, between a difference of understanding in which each side has an excuse and a partisan division in which each side celebrates itself. The verse "and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart" (Quran 8:46) is read the same way, as a ban on quarrelling that breaks ranks, not on the jurist's reasoned opinion.

At Banu Qurayzah the Prophet ﷺ said, "No one should pray the 'Asr prayer except at Banu Qurayẓah," and the party split: some prayed on the road, others waited; "he did not rebuke any one of them" (Sahih al-Bukhari 4119, and Sahih Muslim 1770 with the Zuhr wording). In the tayammum report, two men prayed with dry ablution, then found water within the time; one repeated his prayer and one did not, and the Prophet ﷺ told the one who did not repeat, "You have followed the Sunnah, and your prayer is sufficient for you," while praising the other's extra effort (Sunan an-Nasa'i 433; Sunan Abi Dawud 338, graded sahih by al-Albani with a hasan chain).

The report carrying the weight of the principle is sound: "When a judge gives a ruling and exerts himself in reaching it and gets it right, he has two rewards. And when he gives a ruling and makes a mistake, he has one reward" (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1326, sahih; also Sahih al-Bukhari 7352 and Sahih Muslim 1716, and Sunan Abi Dawud 3574 and an-Nasa'i 5381). Effort in deriving law is rewarded even when wrong, and the error is not a crime.

The Banu Qurayzah instruction, with no rebuke for either group, is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari 4119 and 946 and Sahih Muslim 1770, all sahih, and shows the Prophet ﷺ accepting two contradictory applications of one command. The two travellers and tayammum, both approved, are in Sunan an-Nasa'i 433, sahih, and Sunan Abi Dawud 338, sahih per al-Albani, showing that two different answers to one situation can both be acceptable.

"The Jews divided into seventy-one sects, and my Ummah will divide into seventy-three sects" (Sunan Ibn Majah 3991, hasan sahih; Sunan Abi Dawud 4596 and Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2640, hasan sahih) is a prophecy about division in creed, not a licence for it. "Indeed Allah will not unite my Ummah upon misguidance. The hand of Allah is with the congregation, and whoever departs from it departs to the Fire" (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2167) is graded sahih by Ahmad Shakir but da'if by al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai in the same record, and establishes that the ummah as a whole cannot agree on falsehood.

Two widely quoted sayings are not sound. "The disagreement of my ummah is a mercy" is fabricated (mawdu') per the hadith critics, and al-Albani placed it in al-Silsilah al-Da'eefah. "My Companions are like the stars; whomever of them you follow you will be guided" is fabricated; al-Albani graded it mawdu' and Ibn Hazm rejected its text, so it is not usable as proof even though some fiqh books cite it.

The scholars handled these two without collapsing the principle. Ibn Baz said plainly that "the disagreement of my ummah is a mercy" is not authentic, and traced it to a saying of al-Qasim ibn Muhammad about the Companions' disagreement. Ibn Abidin, writing in a Hanafi book, notes that al-Bayhaqi reported it with a broken chain from Ibn Abbas and still uses its meaning. On "Allah will not unite my Ummah upon misguidance," the grading is disputed inside the same hadith record, but its sense is corroborated by the narration of Abu Busrah that the Prophet ﷺ asked his Lord that his ummah not agree upon misguidance and was granted it, reported by Ahmad and al-Tabari; IslamQA notes that al-Albani graded the Tirmidhi version hasan, which sits awkwardly with the da'if grade in the collection's own apparatus.

The Hanafi school's own text contains the principle in its own words. Ibn Abidin, in Radd al-Muhtar (Hashiyat Ibn Abidin), 1/68, says "The disagreement of the imams of guidance is an expansion for people," citing the report of the first Tatarkhaniyyah; he then quotes Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: had the Companions not differed, there would have been no concession, and Malik's refusal to let Harun al-Rashid impose his Muwatta on the whole ummah because of the scholars' disagreement.

In the Shafi'i school, al-Nawawi (Rawdat al-Talibin, 11/142) reports that in branch matters open to ijtihad there are two positions: the better known is that the truth is one and the mujtahid aims at it, and "the one who takes the other view is mistaken," yet on that same position the mistaken one is forgiven and not sinful; the second position is that every mujtahid is correct. Al-Khatib al-Shirbini (Mughni al-Muhtaj, 6/293) states the wrong one is "mistaken but rewarded for his intent".

The Maliki school's literature is explicit. Al-Qarafi (al-Dhakhira, 1/140-141, quoted by Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyyah) says, "The schools are all paths to Paradise and roads to happiness; whoever takes one of them arrives". Ibn Rushd opens Bidayat al-Mujtahid (1/9) by classifying the six genera of causes of disagreement, from words that are general or particular to shared terminology and elliptical speech, treating variation as a predictable product of the texts, and Malik and al-Layth are reported as saying of the Companions' disagreement that there is in it "expansion and mercy".

Ibn Qudama, in al-Mughni (introduction and 3/23 and 14/145), states the Hanbali position: "Their agreement is a decisive proof and their disagreement a wide mercy". In the prayer chapter he rules that praying behind those who differ in the branches, such as the Hanafis, Malikis and Shafi'is, "is valid and not disliked," citing Ahmad's explicit text, because the Companions and Successors prayed behind one another despite differences, "so that was a consensus"; he adds that the opponent is either correct with two rewards or mistaken with one reward and no sin, and elsewhere that those who differ in the branches are not sinners and their testimony is not rejected.

Al-Buhuti in Kashshaf al-Qina' cites the stars hadith to justify following a less qualified mujtahid, while hadith critics call that report fabricated, so the school's practice rests on the Companions' conduct rather than on that wording. Al-Nawawi's statement in Sharh Sahih Muslim, as quoted by IslamQA, is that differing in deriving the branches is "not forbidden but commanded, and a clear virtue, and the Muslims have agreed on this from the time of the Companions until now".

The first tension is between the verses that condemn division and those that present difference as willed. The resolution is the distinction between ikhtilaf, a difference of route with a shared destination, and khilaf, a difference of both route and destination; the Quran blames the second, and the first is what the Companions practised under the Prophet's ﷺ silence. Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyyah states it as a rule: the branches are open to difference and the definitively established matters are not, and the criterion is whether the text is decisive in transmission and meaning.

The second is between the fabricated "mercy" report and the many sound statements that the scholars' difference carries mercy. Ibn Baz, al-Albani and al-Uthaymeen all refuse the slogan while keeping the substance: the mercy lies in the excuse granted to the mujtahid and in the reward for his effort, and the real mercy is the ummah's consensus, which is protected from error. Ibn Baz adds that "disagreement among scholars contains benefits for the Muslims, even though agreement is better and more excellent", and al-Uthaymeen puts it as: the correct one has two rewards, the mistaken one has one, his error is forgiven, and people cannot be expected to agree on everything because their understanding, knowledge and faith differ.

The third is a direct conflict of readings over Quran 11:118-119. Al-Albani read the exception "except whom your Lord has given mercy" as excluding those who differ from mercy, since the verse's plain sense links mercy to agreement. The more common reading takes the differing ones to be humanity at large in religion, with the exception being those whom Allah guided, and the verse as describing the human condition rather than the status of jurists; both readings are on the record, and the practical conclusions drawn from them differ.

The fourth is internal to the schools. Al-Nawawi reports two Shafi'i positions on whether every mujtahid is correct, and Ibn Qudama records a second Hanbali narration that praying behind someone whose view you consider invalid is not valid, before rejecting it in favour of the practice of the Salaf. The disagreement about disagreement is itself a disagreement, and the schools lived with that too.

Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyyah (fatwa 6293) says there is no harm in the schools' differences in the branches, which are "flexibility, capacity and mercy," and notes that the Companions differed and the Prophet ﷺ did not object; fatwa 6651 (2021) warns against madhhab fanaticism and quotes al-Qarafi's line about the schools as paths; fatwa 6294 says following one specific school is not obligatory, though students are encouraged to study one systematically.

The Permanent Committee's fatwa 4272 traces the disagreement to causes such as a hadith being authentic to one imam and not another, or not reaching him at all, and fatwa 3897 applies the two-rewards hadith to the four imams and to al-Awza'i, al-Thawri and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh. The International Islamic Fiqh Academy's resolution 152 (1/17) of 2006 affirmed that the difference among the schools' followers is in the branches and some principles and is a mercy, and called for avoiding proselytising one school in another's region.

More recent treatments, in 2025 and 2026, repeat that the prohibited thing is tafarruq rather than ikhtilaf, and that denunciation belongs only where a view contradicts a decisive text. The counterweight is equally recent: the "no denunciation in matters of difference" maxim is not absolute. Ibn Uthaymeen divided differences into those genuinely open to ijtihad, where the mujtahid is not blamed but the general public follows its own scholars, and those with no room for ijtihad, where the one who differs is corrected, and Darul Iftaa Chicago, answering a man who wanted to shop between schools on a divorce, advised sticking to one school and not mixing, because picking opinions at will leads to following desire.
